analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 368, Retail Clerks International Association, Local 1625, AFL-CIO et al., Tishners v. Alberta Shermerhorn et al. Mr. Lipman. Thank you, sir. Mr. Chief Justice, and if you please the court, we have a related problem to the one that was just argued before this court. In our situation, the local union and food fair negotiated a collective bargaining contract which contained a panoply of many benefits for the employees. And Florida being one of the right-to-work states, which prohibits the entry into a contract requiring membership in a union pursuant to 14B. How many such states are there? There are 20 at the moment, sir. We negotiated what I think could be correctly characterized as a service fee arrangement. In that service fee, and it's set forth on page 9 of the record, although it's called agency shop, I think the court will recognize that it has substantial differences from the agency shop in the GM case just argued. In that service fee arrangement, we provide that under the law of the state of Florida, the employees have a right to join and not to join the union. However, the union is the exclusive bargaining agent. It's been certified, chosen by the employees. And the union has an obligation under the law to represent all the employees equally and impartially. The union incurs many expenses in connection with its representation. And therefore, we say in so many words, to defray the costs of the union as the collective bargaining agency, employees who determine that they do not wish to join the union would be required to pay a service fee. In a subsequent notice which we posted, after reiterating the language, we said that the service fee would be the equivalent of the monthly dues and the initiation fee. I might point out that the issue before this court and the issue before the Florida Supreme Court was not the amount of the service fee or the reasonableness of the service fee, but was whether or not one penny could be charged as a service fee arrangement. The rationale, if it may please the court, is this. A union has the obligation under the law, and the court has spelled out that obligation, to represent all employees, union and non-union alike, and to represent them impartially. All employees receive these benefits, and the record, the contractors and the record, indicates the substantial benefits involved. Being a collective bargaining agency requires a great deal of expenditures. I think that is clear, and we spelled it out in a brief. One has to hire attorneys and negotiators and full-time representatives. Committees have to be paid. Records have to be kept. Contracts have to be administered. Cases have to be taken to arbitration. And so we say that if you want the benefits, and you have chosen us to obtain benefits for you, we believe that you should pay a prorated cost of carrying on as the collective bargaining agent, not as a member of the union, but as a member of an employee within the bargaining unit. Now, how do we differ from the agency shop? The sums which are paid can only be used to defray the cost of collective bargaining. None of the money could in any way be used for institutional or labor union objectives unrelated to the collective bargaining function of the particular union involved. Which, I suppose, means that these objective employees pay a greater proportion of the collective bargaining cost. No, sir. Why is that? Because the costs of collective bargaining are ascertainable. Just as in a hiring hall arrangement. He's going to pay monthly the same goods the same amount. I mean, as a matter of fact, that was true in this case. In this case, but there is no demonstration... We're talking about this case. Right, sir. In this case, but there's no demonstration in the record that this particular union did not use all of its funds for collective bargaining purposes. This is, after all, a rather small union. It's rather unusual. But this case does not present the question of the reasonableness of the sum. Now, it could very well be that in a subsequent action, in a subsequent proceeding, the reasonableness of the sum could be questioned. Well, are you saying, though, Mr. Littman, that as far as this record is concerned, we have to treat the case as if all union revenues were expended for purposes in carrying on collective bargaining? That is correct, sir. Was there a finding of that effect? There was never any trial. The case was decided on the pleadings. For the purpose of this case, it must be so treated, because this is the sole issue, and this is the sole issue which the court, which lower courts, addressed themselves to. Were the pleadings, the last list, you say, was decided on the pleadings? Yes. The pleadings point out that the employees do not want to be members of the union, they do not want to pay any fees, they do not want to pay any service fees, and that this constitutes a violation of the Florida right-to-work law, and, of course, constitutes a violation section 14B. 46B. Now, I was about to point out, and I think I did point out, that in no sense can any of the monies be used for any institutional purposes, that it can only be used for collective bargaining functions, and that the relationship is the relationship between a union and the employees in a bargaining unit, and not between a union and its membership. Involved here is the question of Section 14 . We'll recess now, Mr. President. Yes. May it please the Court, I sought to develop a forenoon argument that the contract that we have before us, a particular clause, is what we call a service fee arrangement. It's drafted in the sense, and far specifically, that employees in a bargaining unit who choose not to be members of the union must pay a service fee to depray the union's ordinary costs in connection with collective bargaining. We'll also try to make it clear that in issue is not the amount of the fee, but the principle as to whether or not such a clause in a contract can be nullified by the State of Florida operating under Section 14 . I would like now to discuss the requirements and the limitations of 14 as it impinges on the and raises the federal preemption problem. The 14b is quite clear, in that it is an exception to the general pattern of the Labor Act, and provides in substance that the States are permitted to pass laws specifically prohibiting membership in a labor organization. Now, Congress knew quite well what is meant by membership in a labor organization. It is not a difficult, ambiguous word. And if there is any uncertainty about the matter, I believe a reference to the legislative history would demonstrate what Congress was concerned with in 8A3 when they abolished the closed shop, N and 14B. Congress was concerned with the evils of compulsory membership in a union. They were concerned with the Cecil DeMille case, where an employee or a person had to pay assessments for you for political purposes. They were concerned with a situation where an employee was expelled from the union for dual unionism, or an employee lost his job, or an employee who testified against another employee in a court proceeding was expelled from the union. They were concerned with the abuses of internal unionism. In no sense do I find anything in the legislative history which indicates that Congress was concerned with fee payments. To the extent that Congress did have such a concern, it did have an amendment, it does have an amendment in the law, prohibiting excessive initiation fees. Beyond that, there was no concern with that problem. On the other hand, Congress did throughout manifest a concern about the free right. Now, since we have this exception, since the language of 14B is so clear, is a state justified in taking the position that 14B goes beyond what it says, but is a validation of its right-to-work laws? What the states do is they interpret their own laws, and then they say, this stems from 14B, and we have the authority to do so under 14B. Now, what abuses have we seen? We have cases coming from the Supreme Court of South Carolina and Arkansas, outlawing the hiring halt based upon the presumed authority under 14B. We have a case in the Supreme Court of Georgia, where they took the position, where the court took the position, that an exclusive bargaining contract could not stand in face of its right-to-work law, again stemming from the authority of 14B. And we have the opinion of Attorney General in South Dakota to the same extent. The states do not look to the language of 14B, to its intent, but they look to their own right-to-work laws, and under the guise of that, they believe 14B is a license for them to regulate all aspects, or many aspects, of labor relations. In this respect, I raise the question of preemption. Clearly, where a state were to go outside the authority of 14B and say that you cannot negotiate on a particular subject, that you cannot negotiate a hiring halt, or that you cannot negotiate a contract benefiting employees and seeking a service fee in return, where it is not clearly covered by the language, and where quite arguably it is covered by the provisions of the federal act and actually protect it, and where it is not clear at all that the states have such authority, it seems to me if we are going to obtain any kind of uniformity, in the first instance, it should be the labor board, which would have primary jurisdiction to determine whether or not the particular subject matter falls within the scope of 14B and is subject to regulation by the states. Otherwise, we will have at the moment 20 different states, each interpreting 14B and impairing rights under the Labor Act. Well, there may be an element of concurrent jurisdiction. I don't concede it, but I raise the problem. One court, the Supreme Court of Colorado, took the position, the case which we cite in our brief in discuss, took the position that the state merely had the authority to declare the law. And by declaring the law, it could very well nullify the provisos of Section 8A3. Yes. We raise that question because we said, number one, a service fee arrangement, or even an agency shop, is not within the scope of 14B and is covered by the general provisions of the Labor Act, and therefore, of course, the entire area would be controlled by the Labor Act. And in addition, we take the position that where there is an arguable question, a state should not be in a position to sit and determine its own jurisdiction. In this respect, the situation is not entirely dissimilar from the case which this court decided last June, the Meeba case on the Great Lakes, which is opinion written by Justice Potter Stewart. There, a state sought to determine its own jurisdiction by seeking to interpret what is meant by a labor organization within the meaning of the Act, by seeking to interpret what is meant by supervisory employees within the meaning of the Act. But this court held that in the first instance, even there, it is for the Labor Board to determine. And I contend for the proposition that in a situation where a clear question is raised as to whether or not the states have this authority, and where it is also clear, and the question raised, that this comes within the purview of the Labor Board, that in the interest of uniformity and the interest of the preemption principles which have been so thoroughly explored and articulated by this court, it is only the Labor Board which has primary jurisdiction. Otherwise, we will have the most terrible kind of hodgepodge, we will have the most terrible kind of impairment of rights, states interpreting their laws, and saying the authority comes from Section 14.3. Now, we could have a situation of this sort. The state, as the state of Florida, could enjoin the operation of this clause. We could turn around and seek to negotiate a similar clause with the employer. The employer might take the position, as it did in the GM case, that it's, I can't do that, it's outside of the law. The Labor Board might issue a complaint saying that this is outside of the scope of 14.3. And the employer is under an obligation to negotiate on this matter. 14.3. is as much a part of the Labor Act as any other provision. It is a limitation on the board where the states act properly. But the board cannot carry out its functions unless it carries out its functions in light of an interpretation of 14.3. And it is also important that 14.3. be given a uniform interpretation so that all states will interpret and act in the 14.3. in the same way. So don't you think getting a progress to that end might not be possible in this very case? Why should the board have to do it in every case? This is one of the reasons that this court is here. Well, because... What we're dealing with is the meaning of a federal statute. But it's a federal statute over which the board is given exclusive jurisdiction. It's a federal... And the board is given the primary responsibility of protecting rights under the law and tearing out the policies. If the state interprets or passes a law on the 14.3. which impairs any rights under the statute, the board is surely concerned with that. But right here in this case, we have now before us the question of what does Section 14.3. mean? And if certainly there's an opportunity, is there not, to contribute to uniformity by deciding this case. I would say that it would be of great aid to the labor board to interpret 14.3. and give it some definitive meaning. But I would also say that in the final analysis, the determination of whether a service fee arrangement comes within 14.3 or is outside the scope of 14.3 and is therefore a protective kind of activity should be made by the labor board, which is expert not only in the conduct, presumably, but also in the interpretation of the statute. And 14.3 has to be accommodated to the rest of the act. Well, let's assume the state has a law prohibiting a union shop. In the purest sense of that word, I choose whatever language you want for the statute. And if the highest court of the state says this is all it means, it means this and nothing more, and nothing less, do you think it's up to the, do you think the labor board would then have the power of saying, well, I would say in a situation. That means something else, and you have to. I would say, sir, if I understand your question correctly, in a situation where it is absolutely clear, beyond any arguable reason. That's my assumed case. That there, I believe, a state could outlaw or could prohibit the enforcement of that particular clause. But, by an injunction. But there there is, but there there is a great deal of doubt as to whether or not, I mean, taking the reasoning of the, of the Colorado Supreme Court. But, where there is substantial doubt and substantial uncertainty, where the law has been undeclared, then I think only the labor board can make that determination. I don't believe that the principle differs markedly from the principle in any other preemption case. If it is the preemption doctrine that even where the law is well established, where the labor board has set it down, it's well established, that the federal government does not have jurisdiction, then a state has jurisdiction, it would not be necessary to vote to the labor board. I am endeavoring to apply the same principles which this court would apply in any other kind of a preemption case. Now, it seems to me that this court has in a number of cases indicated that 14B does not stand in the way of the application of the preemption doctrine. It's done so recently in the Curry case, which came before this court, where the state of Georgia sought to enjoin activities seeking to obtain a close shop. This court held the application of the preemption doctrine and cited Garmin. This court in the chamber... Mr. Richmond, I really don't understand the right of your reliance and courage why you conceded to Justice White that even in the crystal clear case, the state court granted an injunction against the enforcement of the statute. Well, uh... Because the conduct certainly is an unfair labor practice. Well, the conduct, the conduct is an unfair labor practice. With, uh, I frankly, I don't think anyone knows except as we will learn from this court as to whether or not there is any kind of jurisdiction... Do you find anything in Curry which, uh, suggests that, uh, you should have made that concession? No, sir. I find nothing in Curry which indicates that. As a matter of fact, based on all the indications that I know of, it appears that the state has no authority at all to act in that field except to declare the law. Well, I didn't mean to put words in the matter. Yes. But, uh, but I was... I just wondered whether or not there were... If there was to be any area, if there was to be any area, it isn't that area in which there would be no doubt at all. But, uh, even there, I speak with uncertainty as to just what the authority of the state court is. But surely, and I don't have to go that far, and I only contend for this proposition, surely, in a situation of this kind where there is substantial doubt... About what? ...as to whether or not a service fee arrangement comes under 14B. Or under the state law? Do you think there's any doubt in this case that this kind of arrangement is barred by the Florida law? By the Florida law itself? Well, the, uh, Supreme Court of Florida said, uh, it was barred by the law. And you conceded it in moving to dismiss? Uh, no, we didn't concede that in moving to dismiss. Well, I mean, for the purpose of your motion, dismissing what that is. Well, no, we filed a, uh, we filed a motion, a motion to dismiss was also that, uh, our conduct did not come, uh, uh, was not prohibited by the state law. It was a matter of interpreting the state statute, too. But the question is not, sir, whether or not our conduct could be condemned by the state law, but the question is whether our conduct could be condemned by, uh, by, uh, by section 14b, because whatever validity the state law may have in the field of industry commerce is dependent on section 14b. Suppose 14b had never been adopted, what would you say then? If 14b had never been adopted, uh, again, I would say, uh, in my judgment, there would not have been any doubt that the, uh, that the field was completely preempted. Why? Because... Preempted? Yes. The field would be preempted. What would you say about the legality of the agreement towards the federal law is concerned 14b had not been adopted. It would be a perfectly lawful agreement. Brilliant. Yes. If I understand your question, whether or not an agreement for a service fee arrangement, whether or not that would have been lawful. I'm not talking to you. If you're making a service fee arrangement with the employer, that might be one thing. Making a service fee of employment for employees who do not belong to your union might be another. Well, in this case, sir, we have a service fee arranged with the employer. I... Which is to be paid by the employee who doesn't want to pay it. Which is to be paid by the employee, sir, in order to defray the cost of collective bargaining. There isn't any doubt about its validity under the federal law. The only question which is raised here is the question of the 14B. Because quite clearly, one could justify it under Section 8A5, because the union as a bargaining agent has the power and the authority to provide for its own operations as the exclusive bargaining agent, and in any event, would undoubtedly be saved by Section 8A3, which is a much lesser kind of an arrangement which 8A3 contemplates. So, I would have no doubt that the service fee would be lawful as a matter of federal law. I might say, however, that the only question under the federal law would be as to whether or not, in fact, the service fee was a sincere effort to defray the cost of collective bargaining or whether or not it was an effort to coerce employees into the union. But this is a question of fact which the Labor Board would have to make a determination. Well, suppose you had a record here and you told us we do not. Sorry, sir? Suppose we had a record here and you told us we don't, showing that union revenues were spent for other purposes besides those that are germane in collective bargaining. In that case, sir, there would be a surcharge, there would be a violation of a fiduciary relationship or a violation of trust. The money could be recovered. This money can only be used for collective bargaining purposes and not for any institutional purpose. You've called this very carefully a service fee provision or a service fee arrangement all the way through. Let's assume that it was not that but that it was an agency shock clause as indeed is titled of the purest and most obvious kind similar to the General Motors proposed provision. What do you think that would do? A state could prohibit that under 14B? At this point, I part company with the solicitor. I do not believe the state would have the authority to file that under Section 14B. and the reasons are these. I believe that Section 883 meant what it said that the it is perfectly lawful and permissible for the union to enter into a contract requiring membership in a union and that 883 is a lot more than an agency shop. We have thousands of contracts throughout the country requiring a union shop arrangement, requiring employees to join the union after 30 days of employment. Now, the only problem we have there is that the union shop cannot be enforced in such a way as to jeopardize the employee's job rights so long as he continues to pay his union dues. But that does not mean that he does not have the obligation and that the employer does not have the obligation to see to it that the employee joins the union. Otherwise, Congress just did not say what it meant. One cannot read 883 except by being impressed. It is actually permeated with the idea of membership in the union as a condition of employment. All of the debates indicate that this is a compromise between a closed shop and a union shop. Now, the argument that 14B, therefore, is also an agency shop prohibition stems from that kind of a fallacy that 883 is nothing but an agency shop. but if 883 were in fact, as I believe it to be, a union shop, but with qualifications as to how you can administer it, then the anti-argument would fall because then you could read 14B in its exact language, namely, giving the state's authority only to prohibit membership in the union and not to prohibit any kind of a fee payment. I believe the mistake has been made as a result of the misinterpretation of the union starch case and of radio officers decided by this court because in all of those cases, you have no problem at all about the employee being a member of the union. In my judgment, in my judgment, an employee who says, I refuse to join the union, but I will pay you dues, that employee can be discharged under 883 because he does not have a willingness to join. He can be. Yes, sir. Otherwise, 883 is going to be completely emasculated. But, you cannot impose conditions beyond that. There are two conditions you can impose. One, he must show a willingness to join the union, which is basic. And thereafter, he must pay his union dues and initiation fees. To read an agency sharp out of 883 means that Congress just did not know how to state a simple principle. And I believe this is the error which people have fallen into. Mr. Lippman, you said that there was nothing in the record indicating what the amount of these payments were to be. No, I said there was nothing in the record, how to say, which in any way raised the question of the reason was of the fee. That the only question which was raised is whether or not one penny could be obtained. But we are, I suppose, free to consider the allegations of the complaint, which you didn't controvert in this respect, as to that these payments would be equivalent to initiation fees and monthly dues. That's correct, sir. and so we can't accept those facts anyway. You can accept, yes, you can accept those facts, but whether or not the initiation fees or the equivalent would be used for any other purpose, there you have, there you must also be faced with a proposition. So it's nothing in the record either way on that, whether the union did or did not spend any money for other than collective bargaining. Yes, you do have a record, if I may say so, sir, because the contract itself says it can only be used for the purpose of the frame cost in connection with collective bargaining. And there's no allegation that the money could be or was used in any other respect. And this is the only way in which the union can use the money. That is the only way it can use the service. That's right. The question I put to you is whether there's anything in this record regarding the expenditure of union revenues in gross. Is there anything which indicates that all of the union revenues in gross, whether service fee or otherwise, are all expended for collective bargaining purposes? There's nothing in the record in that respect, sir. Well, you would ask this, I understand it, to consider this record as if all union revenues, inclusive of the service fee revenues, are all used for collective bargaining purposes and nothing else. That's right, sir. And surely... There's nothing in the record to show that. Well, there's nothing in the record to show the contract. Well, we know the facts of life, though. Well, but we say so, sir, with respect to the particular sums collected as service fees, there I only leave one thought, that is this, that that money can only be used for collective bargaining purposes. This means, then, that these people are paying a larger than their proportionate share of the collective bargaining expenses. No, sir, it does not mean that. Because if they were in that position, they would be in the same position that the board was in in the Holman case. They could then come in and object and enjoin the collection of the funds and make sure that all employees were paying the same sums of money for collective bargaining purposes. funds. This is another question entirely. This is a question of the administration, to think. But the sole question we have, and we must assume, that the sums are reasonable and that the sums are only to be used for service fee arrangements and nothing else. the members of the member and the nonmember is in equivalent position in so far as the financial charge to him is concerned. So far as the charge is concerned to him, but not as to the purpose for which the money could be used. The member paying money, sir, his money could be used for institutional purposes. There would be no restriction. but the nonmember, his money could only be used for collective bargaining purposes. Well, this may mean that this is even more burdensome than the union challenge. I don't think so, because he is getting, he is paying, he is paying only what he should pay as a member of the bargaining unit. In any event, the same money comes out of the pocket of the member and the nonmember. Well, the same sum, but with the purposes. That's all, that's my only question. That's right. Mr. Wexler. Mr. Chief Justice, if the court please. In the course of this case, which I have handled from the inception down in Miami, I have heard two startling propositions advanced by the union. One was advanced just before this court a moment ago, the effect that Congress did not know how to state a simple principle. The second startling comment was in the brief that was filed before this court seeking the writ of certiorari when the union boldly stated, in labor relations, as in all other aspects of political life, the power of the purse strings is the power to control. That was stated in the petition for writ of certiorari where the question that was presented to this court and the court considered in granting the writ of certiorari was not a question pertaining to a service fee arrangement. As the union is now seeking to name this particular device or stratagem or gimmick to try to circumvent section 14B and the right to work laws of the state of Florida, the question presented to this court in the petition for the writ of certiorari was whether the Florida Supreme Court misconstrued section 14B of the Taft-Hartley Act in holding that it authorizes the states both to prohibit and to regulate an agency shop clause in an interstate labor contract. After this court granted certiorari, and as I understand the rules of this court, the certiorari is to be limited to the questions presented in the petition for writ of certiorari, then the union switched its attack and now refers to a service fee arrangement, which is supposed to be something separate and distinct from an agency shop. And I will quote the eminent solicitor general when he before referred to a question from Mr. Justice Brennan that there is no difference between an agency shop and a union shop, and I believe he labeled it in Latin as tweedle dum, tweedle dee. I will say that a service fee arrangement is the same thing as an agency shop arrangement on the basis of the record that was presented to the Florida court and the record that is before this United States Supreme Court. The record clearly shows, as Mr. Justice White observed, the complaint. All we had before this court and all we had before the Florida Supreme Court was a complaint wherein the complaint referred to an agency shop provision, wherein the complaint had affixed to it as exhibits, a so-called important notice to employees, which is on page seven of the record, and also had affixed to it as an exhibit on page eight of the record, the particular provision in the union contract referring to an agency shop clause. Nowhere in the contract is there reference to a service fee clause, but always reference to an agency shop clause, and in a petition for rid of certiorari to this court, in 19 places in the petition for rid of certiorari and the brief they referred to an agency shop. Now, what has the union asked for non-union employees of food fair to do? They have told these employees that you do not have to belong to union if you want to work here for food fair. We very graciously say you don't have to belong to union, but if you want to keep on working here as a condition of employment, you must pay to the union the same amount of money that the union member will pay. And because some of the employees of food fair may not be too literate, the union very graciously posted an important notice to the employees to explain the agency shop to these employees and stated because many of you, which notice is page seven of the record, because many of you may not be too familiar with the meaning and purpose of an agency shop, a few words of explanation may be in order. And they explained that under an agency shop, that even though the union and the company have agreed that you may not have joined the union, you are obligated under the provisions of the agency shop to pay an initial service fee, which is the equal of the initiation fee for union members, and a monthly service fee, which is the equal of the monthly dues for those who voluntarily become union members. This is the same provision that is in the General Motors case. They are asked to pay the same amount of money as union members, which is more onerous than the situation that you have with a person who voluntarily becomes a union member. Now, many people, the majority of the people in the state of Florida, and in 19 other right-to-work states, have by election determined that they do not wish to be members of the union. unionism is a matter of voluntary choice.
